sentences.text: Erythromachus leguati, known as the Rodrigues rail, is an extinct bird belonging to the Rallidae family and was endemic to Rodrigues island in the Mascarene Islands.
It was a plump, flightless rail with light grey plumage, possibly spotted with white, a red bill and legs, and a red naked area around its eyes.
The bird measured approximately 35 cm in length and had proportionally longer wings than the red rail.
The bird likely weighed at least 500 grams.
The bird possessed a long beak that curved downwards.
Contemporary accounts state the bird fed on the eggs of three extinct giant tortoise species that lived on Rodrigues.
A phalanx bone of the Rodrigues rail was discovered among fossilized tortoise egg remains.
Reports suggest the bird was attracted to red objects, which made it easier for humans to catch them.
Specialized rails like the Rodrigues rail could evolve flightlessness and distinct features in less than 1 to 3 million years.
The species was first documented by Leguat in a memoir published in 1708.
Hugh Edwin Strickland drew attention to the bird in François Leguat's 1708 memoir in 1848.
Subfossil remains were discovered and linked to historical accounts in 1874.
The Rodrigues rail was flightless and fed on tortoise eggs.
It fed on invertebrates and possibly small vertebrates, and during the nesting season of the extinct giant tortoises, it dug up and fattened their eggs.
It likely fed on worms like Kontikia whartoni and Geonemertes rodericana by probing leaf litter or rotting wood.
They had no fear of humans because they evolved in the absence of predators, allowing hunters to catch them in large numbers.
Its vocalizations included a continuous whistle and an alarm call resembling a hiccup.
The fat of birds that had fed on turtle eggs was bright orange and used as a remedy for people recovering from illness.
Günther and E. Newton confirmed in 1879 that the bird belonged to the rail family.
Günther and E. Newton synonymized the two rails into one genus in 1879 due to skeletal similarities.
The species is generally placed in the genus Erythromachus but has sometimes been grouped with the red rail in Aphanapteryx.
The genus was established by Milne-Edwards in 1874.
The genus Erythromachus lived during the Holocene, from 0.0117 to 0 million years ago.
Julian Hume suggested the ancestors arrived in the Mascarenes no earlier than the middle Miocene, though it may have been more recent.
Geoffroy Atkinson questioned the bird's existence in 1921 by doubting the truth of Leguat's memoir.
American ornithologist James Greenway suggested that Leguat's description referred to the common crab, but this has not been accepted by other authors.
Researchers noted significant variation in beak shape and length among specimens but debated whether this indicated sexual dimorphism or individual size differences.
Hume and Walters suggested the species went extinct within a decade of cat introduction around 1750, though the exact cause remains debated.
